title: Gateless Barrier, Case 42: Manjusri and the Young Woman in Samadhi
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up Case 42 of the Gateless Barrier, in which Manjusri, the bodhisattva of wisdom, cannot rouse a woman sitting in samadhi near the Buddha's throne, and the earthy Ensnared Light wakes her with one finger snap. Nomon recalls a Samish sesshin evening when a woman stayed motionless in zazen after everyone left, until Norman Fischer softly touched her shoulder. Suzuki Roshi's words on practice and enlightenment and the image of snow sliding off a roof or melting slowly shape a look at stages versus gradual waking. Nomon reads the case as a reminder to seek wise friends who can snap us out of our trances, friends who are a bit of a mess themselves. A poem by the early nun Muta, about her first bite of food as a free woman, closes the evening.

Tonight we have case 42 from the Mu Mon Kong collection.

And this one's like a really far out story.
Here's the case.
Once in the old days, in the time of the World Honored One, Monju Sri went to the assembly of the Buddhas and found that everyone had departed to their original dwelling place.
Only a woman remained, sitting in samadhi, close to the Buddha's throne.
Monju Sri asked Chakyamuni Buddha, "Why can the girl get near the Buddha's throne while I cannot?"
Chakyamuni Buddha said, "Bring her out of samadhi and ask her yourself."
So Monju Sri walked around the girl three times, snapped his fingers once, and took her to the Brahma heaven.
And there exerted all his miraculous powers to bring her out of her meditation.
But in vain.
The World Honored One said, "Even a hundred thousand Monju Sri's cannot make her wake up."

We have a presumably ordinary, but seasoned human practitioner, who isn't named, but she's referred to as the woman.
Second we have the Shakyamuni Buddha, who is the Buddha we think of, the Buddha of our age.
Third we have Monju Sri, who is like a super duper Bodhisattva.
I think we would probably think of him as a god, or maybe a demigod.
Not really a human figure actually, but maybe taken a human shape.
And Monju Sri is usually spoken of with a male pronoun, but I don't know why he or she would exactly have gender.
She, let's say.
Monju Sri is the embodiment of wisdom, so just pure and transcendent and brilliant, and just always knowing what to do, super brilliant and wise.
And then fourth we have this strange entrance from another figure towards the end.
Another Bodhisattva, but kind of a lesser Bodhisattva we're going to find out later.
Bodhisattva called Ensnared Light, who is not like in the Buddha's hall and not in the heavens that they go off to.
He or she is in the earth.
He's like in the dirt.
So now you can have a sense of who the four figures are.
This is a pretty far out story, I'll read the story again, so it'll probably land a little more clearly.
Once in the old days, in the time of the World Honored One, Monju Sri went to the assembly of the Buddhas and found that everyone had departed to their original dwelling place.
And only a woman remained, sitting in Samadhi, close to the Buddha's throne.

So there are a lot of things that are interesting here, so we'll take a little time unpacking.
Don't worry.
First, the interesting thing is that Monju Sri is traditionally seen as like the teacher of the Buddhas.
But here, the places are reversed, and the Buddha seems to be really in the teacher role.
The comment from Master Wu Men, who collected these cases into the book, is kind of interesting there.
Wu Men says, "Old Shakyamuni Buddha put on a petty drama on the stage and failed to enlighten the masses."
I want to ask you, Monju Sri is the teacher of the seven Buddhas.
Why couldn't he arouse the woman from her Samadhi?
How was it that a Bodhisattva at the beginner's stage could do this?
If you understand this intimately, you can enjoy Nagya's Grand Samadhi in the busiest activity of consciousness.
Monju Sri is the teacher of the seven Buddhas.
He couldn't accomplish this thing that they're talking about, which we'll explore.
And yet there's this other Bodhisattva who Wu Men says was at the beginner's stage.
He could do it.
So it turns out there are stages and levels.
There are systems for everything, including in Buddhism.
Do not think that Buddhism is free from systems.
So there are traditionally eight stages of development in the career of a great Bodhisattva.
And the later entrance, the Bodhisattva in Snared Light, is at the first level only, which is probably where we're at.
We're probably at the half level or something like that, us, but we're Bodhisattvas too.

But before that, before the appearance of Bodhisattva in Snared Light, we have this interesting situation with this woman that she has entered a deep and powerful concentration state in meditation, a Samadhi, S-A-M-A-D-H-I, Samadhi.
And she's just in it.
She's concentrated.
She's deep in practice, and she can't be sort of shook out of it back to her normal consciousness, at least not till the end of the story.
She can't be roused.
She's in too deep.
And this is actually a real thing that happens.
Not often, but this is a real thing that happens.
I've seen this happen.
We had someone once get stuck in Samadhi at our Samish sesshin, our annual June sesshin retreat.
I still remember that really well.
It was in the evening.
We sat a period of Zazen, and the bell rang to end and get up for Kinhan.
And this woman, it was also a woman, didn't move, just sat there very still.
And we did our walking meditation, and she kept sitting very still.
We did Zazen again, and she kept sitting.
And then the bell rang for the last Zazen period of the evening, where we get up and do prostrations and chanting like we'll do tonight.
And she still didn't move.
And everyone left, was leaving the hall for the evening to go to bed.
Usually it's a pretty long day, so usually at the end, people are pretty much eager to get out of there.
They want to go lie down in the kitchen, or I don't know what they all do.
But they're done.
They're out of there.
But she's still sitting perfectly still in Zazen.
So I realized I should ask my teacher, Norman Fischer, our founding teacher, who lives in California, that I should ask him to help.
Ask him to help kind of try to bring her out of it.
Because what are we going to do?
We can't just leave her stuck in Samadhi, right?
So I asked him to do this, and I watched from kind of across the room.
And I felt like I probably didn't know how to do it right.
I might really mess her up or something if I just shook her or pinched her cheek or something.
And we also have this deep sense in the meditation hall of just leaving people be, right?
It's silent.
You don't touch people or talk or anything.
But anyway, I watched Norman go over there very slowly, speaking softly as he approached her.
I think he kind of gently touched her on the shoulder and talked to her softly.
And I didn't hear what he said.
But she did come out of it.
I don't totally remember what happened next, but I think she kind of blinked a few times and then just got up, put on her coat and walked out.
Just left, as if nothing strange had happened.
In a way, it's not so strange, though, actually.
We all have moments where we are in it, right?
Whatever it is, you know?
Forgetting ourselves, whether it's deep in concentration or deep in distraction or just deep in something, the mind is such a rich terrain, right?
Our usual conventional kind of bouncing around and doing stuff is only one of so many ways we can be in this mind, in this body.
And some of the meditation systems suggest that there are a series of deep meditation states, kind of trance states, jhanas, dhanas, samavis.
There's different names for them that you can go through in the course of your career as a meditator, maybe ultimately leading to some final realization or awakening or enlightenment.
And that kind of makes sense to us, right?
There should be a plan, right?
You should have to do this, then this, then this.
But other systems of meditation don't really see it that way.
And maybe those systems, it's just one whole but mysterious process without steps or stages.

I think oftentimes people in that system see the idea of steps and stages as sort of like a little problematic, a little distracting, maybe a cause of suffering or confusion because of the way we're so conditioned to try to get it right and do better and so on.
And as Dogen, the Japanese founder of our school, said so beautifully in so many ways, we really can't measure or understand our zazen.
Our enlightenment is not usually about flashing lights and dramatic experiences.
It's kind of a waking up, you know?
And that can be called sudden or called gradual or called anything, but it's really just waking up.
Waking up to who we are, to what this all is.
And it's also kind of a sloughing off, right?
You know, it's not like getting something.
It's mostly a releasing of stuff.
A sloughing off of so many layers of suffering and conditioning and fear and all of it, right?
We all know what this stuff is.
Confusion, clinging.
And sometimes that sort of sloughing off process is a little bit like when the snow builds up on the roof pretty deep.
Sometimes it just goes off all at once, right?
Like the bottom layer gets melted and goes whoosh.
And it's big and it's dramatic and it's loud.
I don't have that in Bellingham as much, but if you've ever experienced that, if you live somewhere snowy or up in the mountains in the winter, it's intense, you know?
But other times or more often, most times actually, I think, it's more like the sun just gradually melts the snow on the roof, you know, or encasing you.
And maybe your friends notice that you seem lighter and less preoccupied, less worried, maybe a little more present.
You may not notice anything at all, right?
Because we're so used to thinking we are who we are and we know what that's like and the inner narrative goes on, blah, blah, blah.
That means sometimes your friends or your loved ones say, "Hey, you seem different somehow.
What was that?"
And maybe you likely as not just try to kind of brush that off, "Oh, now I'm just the same old me."
Of course we're changing, right?
Everything changes, including us.
And practice is a support for a certain kind of change.
Well, maybe sometimes we do notice changes even within the middle of the confusion of our own perspective, you know?
Maybe you catch yourself being a little less reactive or more flexible or saying or doing something that seems somehow perceptive or wise.
"How do I think to say that to her?
You know, wow.
Did that or okay?
Oh, wow, good."
And so sometimes this path of practice does include all kinds of experiences.
How could it not, right?
We're nothing but experiences.
That's what life is, is experiences.
And so people experience these samadhis of various kinds.
And in Buddhism there's descriptions and systems and typologies and taxonomies of samadhi this and samadhi that.
There's a whole ton of them.
I don't even know what they all are.
But for most of us, actually, a lot of us, maybe most of us, this path doesn't include big dramatic experiences being stuck in samadhi.
Sometimes I think, well, maybe it just has to do with sort of different neurological wiring.
Some people are more prone to it, you know?
Like people are prone to different things.
Sometimes it's actually about stress, actually.
When meditators are in like high stress situations, they're more likely to have intense experiences and visions just like in normal life, right?
If you're under a lot of stress, weird shit happens, right?
And either the meditator is in a high stress situation in their life and then they finally make it to the meditation retreat and whoosh, you know, down comes the snow off the roof.
Or sometimes in the system of meditation training there's high stress that's designed in.
You know, there's an induction, stress induction.
A lot of stress in hopes of some kind of like breakthrough or something.
And of course, we're all conditioned to be drawn to and interested in drama, right?
Literally drama, like stories.
We understand life and everything to be like a story with a beginning, a middle, and an end, with a heroic struggle, with a victory at the end.
So that fits that model, right?
Some kind of intense effort in meditation, some kind of samadhi, some kind of breakthrough.
That sounds awesome.
And just ordinary, everyday, gradual, don't know if this is working at all, that doesn't always sound so exciting, you know?
But maybe in a certain way it's healthier, you know?
And that's what we emphasize, of course.
So of course I think it's better because I'm conditioned, too.

So it's hard to even get your mind around some of that, right?
What would be beyond your experience of good and bad?
It's worth really spending some time trying to imagine that, or musing about that.
So readily we turn things into good and bad, right?
All the time.
So fast.
When he says selfish, he used selfish in a way that doesn't land as well, I think, in our decade.
Yeah, he meant self-focused or self-centered or self-oriented.
You're trying to get something for yourself.
Which in a way there's nothing wrong with taking care of yourself, of course.
But you know what I mean.
What are you saying?
And it's interesting too, when I started practicing Zen in the mid-80s, it was like kind of forbidden to talk about your meditation experiences.
You weren't supposed to.
It was very private.
I assume the intention was to avoid confusion and to really kind of honor the, you know, sort of sacredness of the practice.
And also have the relationship with the teacher be really the central thing.

and a certain kind of grasping that arises around anything.
It can especially arise around anything that seems special.
After meditation or during a retreat, someone seems a little bit like glowing, or has a nice smile.
You might wonder, "Is he getting something I'm not getting?" or "Do you have an experience?"
I just sat there worrying about all kinds of stuff and being bothered by my knee, thinking, "What a waste of time for me.
And he's getting something."
I think we were all sort of thinking that then.
I remember experienced students who were around me.
I was young, but I remember people quite a bit older and more experienced making positive, usually judgmental comments about other people's practice.
I remember where it was a sheen, and I was on the meal serving crew, so we were able to talk a little bit in the context of the meal serving crew; otherwise, the retreats are silent.
This other woman kind of walked by the other end of the hallway, or somewhere we could see, and just looked very upright and dignified, settled, and she looked beautiful too.
I remember the meal leader saying, "Wow, she looks concentrated."
And somehow we were all like, "Okay, okay, that's what we're supposed to do.
Got to get that."
The narrative that arises from there is, "Okay, she is getting it, but I don't, right?"
So, "I suck.
I'm no good at this," or "The whole thing sucks," or "The teacher sucks," or "The whole thing's just a crock of whatever."
Most of us default to, "I suck," which is so damaging—such deep conditioning in us that we feel we're not good enough, that we'll never be good enough.
I'm just grateful that we maybe have a little more of an open and curious stance now, and a little less dualistic, like there's a better or a worse way to practice.
We're all just doing our best.
Whether the snow is melting slowly or sloughing off in great rushes, what's the real difference in the end?
Still snow melting, still people healing and growing and changing.
One little backstory on this woman in Samadhi requires some explanation.
Before we even meet her, we have a different problem.
Manjushri in this has many problems.

In the opening lines, it says, "Once in the old days, in the time of the World Honored One, Manjushri went to the assembly of the Buddhas and found that everyone had departed to their original dwelling place."
This must have been a big bummer.

Manjushri showed up at the assembly—which is like the central meeting hall for all the Buddhas and the students and the Bodhisattvas—and you could picture it as an ordinary building or a transcendent place.
They had already left.
It was like showing up for Wednesday night's Auzhan at seven and there was just a little note on the screen that said, "We're all enlightened, see ya.
Keep the place warm for us."
That's what "original dwelling place" means; they're all enlightened.
But not everyone is gone.
After getting over the shock, Manjushri looks around and sees this human woman sitting so peacefully, so powerfully, like the woman I saw walking way back.
It says, "The only woman remains sitting in Samadhi close to the Buddha's throne."
That means she's literally close to Buddha, close to awakening—it's a positive judgment of her practice, super practice.
It is interesting and noteworthy that even though she's not named, the figure is female, so a little bit of props to the ancestors there.
That woman practiced just as deeply as men, as deeply as any kind of gender identity; it's not dependent on that, but she's in deep meditation.
Apparently, Manjushri is not happy that all the other bodhisattvas are gone, and he's a little jealous of this woman's apparent meditative accomplishment.
Using the same symbolism of sitting near the Buddha's throne, he asks the Buddha, who is also there—so there are three of them there right now—"Why can this girl get near the Buddha's throne?
Well, I cannot."
The Buddha says, "Bring her out of her Samadhi and ask her for yourself."
This is back to talking about our practice, a little different from what I was saying.
"Ask her for yourself.
I'm not going to explain it to you."
This is healthy, I think.
We can ask each other about our practice, and we need to be reflective and careful, saying only what we've experienced, not what we imagine.
"How's meditation going for you?
What are you finding?
What are you noticing?
What's the feeling of it?"
It's hard to put words on it, of course, because it's a little bit beyond words, but we can ask each other.
Manjushri wants to ask her, and instead of shaking her on the shoulder first, he shows off a little bit.
He walks around the girl three times, snaps his fingers once, and takes her to the Brahma heaven.
The whole scene just rematerializes in the heavens.
There are heavens in Buddhism, and then it says he exerted all his miraculous powers to bring her out of her meditation, but in vain.
He made magical things happen; they could generate lights and energy beams shooting out of their foreheads and fingers.
This is all in the traditional texts.
It's pretty far out; they can make Buddhas appear in floating flowers, and then there are Buddhas inside the fingernails of the Buddhas in the floating flowers and all kinds of stuff.
None of this is she even interested in.
She's not distracted by it; she's not brought out of her samadhi by it.
She's just there, deeply being.
Poor Manjushri.
You can't get even this ordinary human woman to pay attention to him, even though he can do all these incredible powers.
No dice.
The Buddha watches all this, probably a little amused, and says, "Even a hundred thousand Manjushris cannot make her wake up."
But down below, past one thousand two hundred million lands as innumerable as the sands in the Ganges, there is a Bodhisattva called Ensnared Light.
He will be able to rouse her from her samadhi.
This is interesting.
Manjushri, as you know, is this Bodhisattva—top-level Bodhisattva, transcendent wisdom Bodhisattva, manifestation of wisdom beyond wisdom.
He's like the top, clear and insightful, and just glowing and wondrous, and just knows what's needed, discerning.
Manjushri is often pictured with a sword because he's so discerning; he just cuts right through anything with wisdom, not with violence.
But that's not what's needed here.
We don't need transcendent wisdom right now.
Maybe what we need is something a little more earthy, maybe a little messier, maybe a little more tangled up.
In one translation, the Bodhisattva who's called forth, who lives in the earth, is called Ensnared Light.
It must be some hard characters to translate here because I saw several different translations for the name of this Bodhisattva.
One was "seed of delusion."
Another was "delusive wisdom."
And then this name I find really interesting is "ensnared light."
So there's light here, there's wisdom here, but it's tangled, it's ensnared, it's delusive, it's messy.
Does this sound familiar to you?
It's just like us, right?
It's earthy; it's not all pure.
It's a little bit messed up, but it's also light, it's also wisdom, it's also potential, it's also awakening.
So the Buddha says, "Yeah, it doesn't matter how many Manjushris you get on the project here; that's just the wrong deal.
We need something else."
Instantly, because the Buddha called it forth, the Bodhisattva Ensnared Light emerged from the earth and made a bow to the World Honored One who gave him his imperial order.
It's a funny translation.
I think the Buddha just pointed at the woman and said, "You know, dear thing."
The Bodhisattva went over to the woman and snapped his fingers once, and at this, she came out of Samadhi.
She responded to this figure with darkness in him or her or they.
She responded much better to the luminous, perfect wisdom.
That's where the story ends, at least in the Koan collections.
We don't find out if Manjushri got to ask her what was up and how she did this practice where she was close to the Buddha's throne in this deep Samadhi.
The commentaries say this is an excerpt of a longer story and a sutra, but I don't think it's been translated as far as I can figure out.
This is also a reminder to us that we're barely grazing the surface here with our studies.
Buddhist literature is just vast—Chinese literature, Indian literature, Tibetan literature, old Indian literature.
So many texts and stories and teachings.
I don't know what percent of it's been translated to be five percent, maybe something like that.
And then we've maybe scraped five percent of the five percent, something like that.
But it's okay, because Dogen says this over and over again: "Just to practice one thing, just to study one thing, just to see clearly in one moment, that's enough."
This isn't about encyclopedic knowledge; it isn't about learning lots and lots and lots of stuff.
It's about clarity.
It's about vision.
It's about letting that stuff slough off.
Another way to look at this story that's very practical, I think, is it's about the many ways we get entranced.
Don't you think we don't always notice it when we're doing it?
In fact, we often don't notice this when we're doing it.
We can get so easily caught up in all kinds of ideas, views, desires, hopes, our powerful beliefs about who we are, and who we aren't, and who they are, and how it's supposed to work.
We actually need friends.
It's like the woman; it's also sort of assumed in that story that she would just stay in that samadhi forever, and if you don't eat, it's still a problem even if you're a great meditator.
So we need a friend sometimes to snap us out of it.
Whether it's a beautiful vision, a powerful, lovely meditation state, like, "Okay, you've been in there for a few hours now, or a few days, why don't you come eat?"
Or if it's a really difficult state, a deep confusion, a delusion, and samadhi does not have a positive or negative value judgment in it.
Suzuki Roshi was saying it's beyond good or bad.
Samadhi is kind of like this container of concentration that you're within, like a barrier.
Barriers aren't all bad; sometimes you need barriers, right?
Sometimes barriers are a big problem.
One of the places you can have a lot of difficult samadhi, I have experiences in, is when there's powerful turmoil in relationships, or powerful turmoil of any kind.
It's so easy to just convince yourself deeply of some story about what's going on, or what's supposed to be happening, what isn't supposed to be happening.
Over the last couple of years, I've had a lot of relationship turmoil in particular, and convinced myself of various things at different times.
In a few cases, I was so helped, so helped.
I can't believe how much I was helped by having a wise friend there.
A wise friend snapped their fingers for me.
One case I was just thinking of was a friend of mine whose version of the finger snap was just to have like the right kind of respectful skepticism.
Do you know, do you have this kind of friend who'd be kind of like, "Really?
You sure about that?"
Sometimes just, bam, you wake up, "Oh, jeez, what was I thinking?"
Of course, it's not that way, really.
It's caught an idea there, caught in desire, caught in vision, caught in a plan.
Samadhi is not inherently good or bad; it's just that the mind can create powerful states where there's some kind of stability.
And the stability can actually exist around or with powerful instability.
Again, it's kind of a container; samadhi, concentration is another translation.

This is a wonderful thing and a potentially damaging thing, so it's worth really thinking about who your friends and family members, supporters, who help you in this way, who can snap their fingers and help you wake up a little more.
Maybe what they're doing is whacking the roof with a broom to get some of the snow down for you.
If you aren't seeking out friends like that or spending time with friends like that, of course it's harder now.
Maybe that's really important—that actually should be more of a priority to have wise friends who can snap their fingers for you.
It's not always what you want to hear at the time, right?
We like our delusions; we like our dreams and fantasies.
We must, or else why would we get caught by them?
But we always feel much better in a deeper way, an open way, a softer way, when we wake back up to something that's more like reality, for want of a better word.
The other thing about this, though, is that our friends with the finger snap, this story is correct, and I think it is.
They shouldn't be too perfect either.
When you're caught in some kind of state, you don't want a perfect, luminous friend, right?
The one who always gets everything right and is so smart and never screws up like you do.
A friend is a bit of a mess too.
That's the wisdom maybe of this story: that our wise helpers can also be a bit of a mess.
We probably also need the luminous ones, the Manjushris, the perfect-looking people, even though of course they're not.
That's also our delusion.
But I think we especially need the people who are more like a compassionate mess, a wise mess.
That's my attempt to unpack case 42.
That's a lot in there, huh?
